title: Cryptosporidium Transmission in the United States: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: Cryptosporidiosis is a gastrointestinal illness where patients experience watery diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain, fever, and weight loss that can linger for up to three weeks in immunocompetent patients. In immunocompromised patients, symptoms are much more severe and persist for a longer duration. A cross-sectional study was done to assess the effect of region and season on the number of cases reported to the CDC in 2022. The dependent variable was cryptosporidium cases and independent variables were region and season. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was done in assessing statistical significance (P<.05), effect size, and pairwise comparisons. Findings revealed statistical significance for both region and season, Partial Eta squared of 0.791 for region and 0.660 for season. For pairwise comparisons analyzing transmission across regions, the northeast was significantly different from south, southwest, and Midwest; south was significantly different from northeast and southwest; southwest was significantly different from northeast, south, and Midwest; Midwest was significantly different from northeast and southwest. For transmission across seasons, winter was significantly different from summer and fall; spring was significantly different from summer; summer was significantly different from winter, spring, and fall; fall was significantly different from winter and summer. These findings add to the body of knowledge regarding cryptosporidium transmission and provide insight into seasonal and regional patterns of infectivity in future outbreaks.
